props.title: Killer Fish

sections.content: **Killer Fish** (1979) belongs to the wild wave of aquatic horror that followed **Jaws** (1975). This Italian-Brazilian exploitation film, directed by Antonio Margheriti (under his pseudonym Anthony M. Dawson), stars Lee Majors and Karen Black in a bizarre hybrid of heist thriller and creature feature. The plot follows jewel thieves who stash their loot in a reservoir infested with deadly piranhas - a premise that shamelessly combines elements of **The Deep** (1977) and Piranha (1978). The film exemplifies the "anything goes" spirit of late 70s international co-productions chasing the creature feature craze.

sections.content: The late 1970s saw an explosion of aquatic horror films trying to replicate the success of **Jaws** (1975). Italian producers were particularly prolific, churning out titles like Tentacles (1977), **Orca** (1977), and **Great White** (1981). These films often featured fading Hollywood stars, exotic locations, and varying degrees of technical competence. **Killer Fish** stands out for its unusual blend of crime thriller elements with creature feature conventions, predating similar genre mashups like **Deep Blue Sea** (1999).

The film's practical effects, while dated, represent a particular era of pre-CGI creature features where mechanical props and creative editing had to sell the terror. The piranha attacks follow a pattern established by Italian horror maestros like Lucio Fulci, emphasizing graphic gore over suspense. This approach contrasts sharply with Spielberg's technique of suggesting violence through reaction shots in **Jaws** (1975). SUBHEAD: The Italian Connection

sections.content: Director Antonio Margheriti was a veteran of Italian genre cinema, known for his work in science fiction (**Wild, Wild Planet** [1966]) and horror (**Cannibal Apocalypse** [1980]). His approach to **Killer Fish** reflects the Italian film industry's talent for maximizing production value on modest budgets through creative location shooting and international casting. The Brazilian setting provides exotic appeal while serving the practical needs of a water-heavy production.
